tracks.title: One machine, two audiences
tracks.text: Lesson zero two point five — planes. This one is a sub-lesson, under nexus. One machine, two audiences. Your Nexus is the most privileged thing you own — secrets, agents, build tools, the Dock. And now you want to take a single page out of it… and put that page on the open internet, where the least-trusted requests on Earth will hammer it. [curious] Every instinct says those two facts are incompatible. The dread is specific… and correct. If my published site and my engine share a machine… then a request to the site is a request to the engine. This lesson is the other answer. Same box… both audiences… and the wall between them is not a proxy you can misconfigure. It's the absence of a road.

tracks.title: Two planes, one node
tracks.text: Two planes, one node. So what is a plane? A plane is a complete, separate HTTP surface — its own listener, its own router, its own trust posture — running on the same node as the others. There are two of them. First, the control plane — it is authenticated… and it does things. Second, the content plane — it is anonymous, GET-only… and it serves bytes. Two separate routers, two separate listeners, one BEAM node. The control plane is where deploys, the Dock, agents, builds, and key escrow live — every one of them behind a single authentication plug. The content plane has none of that. And more importantly… it has no code that could do any of it. One plane to operate the engine. One plane to publish from it. And a hard line drawn between them.

tracks.title: Security by routes that don't exist
tracks.text: Now the move that makes this safe — and it's not the move you'd guess. Security by routes that don't exist. The content plane isn't the engine with auth bolted on. There is no auth plug on it at all — and there doesn't need to be… because there's nothing on that plane to protect. No Dock route. No build. No commands. No agents. No secret escrow. Those code paths aren't guarded on the content plane — they are absent from it. [excited] Picture two routers side by side. On the control plane, the very first line is a single plug — Auth — and it gates the entire router. Everything below it needs a credential. On the content plane… no Auth at all. Just match, dispatch, and one catch-all at the bottom: any request that isn't a GET lands on a single line that answers four-oh-four. A POST doesn't get rejected by a rule. It has nothing to match… so it can't do anything. And here's the payoff. The question — what can an anonymous request reach on the public internet? — is answered by reading one file, end to end. About five hundred and thirty lines. And confirming the dangerous verbs simply aren't in it. [chuckles] Absence is the easiest property in the world to check.

tracks.title: How the planes come up
tracks.text: How do the planes come up? Each one is opt-in… so a bare boot binds nothing. You turn a plane on with an environment variable. First — WB underscore WEB equals one… turns on the control plane, on port four thousand. Second — WB underscore PUBLIC equals one… turns on the content plane, anonymous and GET-only, on port four thousand and one. Third — WB underscore PUBLIC underscore TLS equals one… turns on HTTPS for the content plane, on port four-four-four-three, and installs the per-domain cert callback we'll get to shortly. One more detail, because it surprises people. Every listener is dual-stack — it binds both IPv6 and IPv4 on one socket. The reason is concrete. Private platform networks between cloud machines are IPv6-only… while a local client on your laptop dials IPv4. One dual-stack socket serves both… without a second listener.

tracks.title: The host is the address
tracks.text: The host is the address. On the content plane, the path doesn't pick the app — the host header does. A function called resolve takes the incoming hostname and answers with an app id. A registered host wins outright. And if the host isn't registered, the rule is dead simple — the leftmost DNS label is the app. So demo dot apps dot example… resolves to the app named demo. Picture the whole exchange as a short conversation. The browser asks for the root of demo dot apps dot example. The plane hands that hostname to resolve… and gets back the app, demo. It reads that app's static tree off the durable volume. And it returns the bytes — stamped with an honesty header and a comment. The path never named the app. The host did. And that one-origin-per-app rule is the real tenant wall — and it's the browser's wall, not ours. Because each app lives on its own origin, its JavaScript is bound by same-origin policy. It can never read or ride a cookie belonging to the control plane… because that plane lives on a different hostname entirely. The browser enforces it… for free.

tracks.title: An honest surface
tracks.text: An honest surface. Every response the content plane sends identifies itself. There's a header set on the way out — x dash served dash by… workbooks dash runtime. And every HTML page gets a comment injected before the closing head tag, saying it was served by the Workbooks runtime, public content plane. That's the header and the view-source comment you've probably already noticed. They're not branding — they're a standing claim about what served you, verifiable from outside with one curl. The plane also hosts two anonymous, read-only feeds. The first — underscore changes — returns the app's real git log, newest-first, capped at thirty entries, plus the keeper's status. It mirrors an authed route on the control plane… with one difference that's the whole point. It resolves the app from the public host… not from a tenant credential. The published app serves its own verifiable history… to anyone… without logging in. The second feed — underscore activity — goes one layer deeper: keeper status, a tail of step telemetry, and a narration thought. Both feeds return four-oh-four, with the message no app for host, when the hostname doesn't resolve.

tracks.title: One node, many domains
tracks.text: Now the aha that retires the reverse proxy. One node, many domains. The thing people run Caddy or nginx for — serving many custom domains, presenting the right certificate for whichever one is dialed — turns out to be one function. Erlang's TLS layer takes a callback. On every handshake it hands you the hostname the client asked for… and you hand back the cert to present. Wire that callback to a lookup… and one BEAM node serves any number of domains. The constraint that shapes everything is where that callback runs — inside the TLS acceptor, on every single handshake. So it must be fast… and it must not block. It absolutely cannot call into a GenServer — a slow reply would stall every pending handshake behind it. So the registry uses a deliberate split. Reads hit an ETS table directly, lock-free, no process hop. Writes serialize through a single GenServer… so there's exactly one writer. Picture the handshake as a story. The client says hello and names the host it wants — app dot acme dot com. The acceptor calls the cert function with that name. The function reads ETS directly and finds the row. It returns the cert and key file paths. The handshake completes. And only now… does an HTTP request exist for the content plane to serve.

tracks.title: The handshake is the bouncer
tracks.text: The handshake is the bouncer. The same lookup that picks the cert… is also the admission gate. When the cert function is handed a host that isn't registered, it returns an empty list. With no cert to present… the TLS handshake cannot complete. A stranger doesn't get a four-oh-three page. They don't get a four-oh-four. They don't get an HTTP response at all — because there is no TLS session for HTTP to ride on. Rejection happens before HTTP exists. Picture the lifecycle as three states. First — unknown — every host starts here. Second — pending — once you attach the host to a tenant and an app. Third — live — once you install a certificate with put cert. An attached host completes its handshake cleanly. An unknown one… returns the empty list, and fails at the transport layer. And there's a deliberate refusal baked in here. Certs are issued on attach… not on handshake. Caddy's on-demand model issues a certificate the first time anyone dials a hostname — which turns your server into a cert mill an attacker can drive by spraying random names. So here, a verified attach happens first, the cert is provisioned out of band… and only an already-issued cert ever gets presented inside the millisecond budget of a handshake. The two-step isn't bureaucracy. It's the anti-footgun.

tracks.title: The shape in production
tracks.text: The shape in production. workbooks dot s-h eats this dogfood — this very lesson is served by the content plane. The deployed reference is a single fly config, for the app wb dash site, running the same runtime image you'd run, with a durable volume at slash data. Walk the config. The env block turns the content plane on, points it at the wb dash site directory, and sets the public port to four thousand and one. Then two service stanzas. The first — public — maps eighty and four-forty-three to internal four thousand and one, the content plane. Auto-stop is off… because an origin can't go to sleep between visitors. The second — control — sits on port four thousand, exposed but locked by a two-hundred-fifty-six-bit bearer secret. Present it and you're in. Absent or wrong… and it's a flat four-oh-one, with no dev fallback. Two services… two planes… exactly the split this lesson draws. And one honest framing about the reverse proxy. There's no proxy between the planes — that's the claim this lesson makes good on. But Cloudflare does sit in front of the whole node as an edge, and Fly terminates the public TLS itself. That's not a contradiction. A lone BEAM machine can't self-defend against a volumetric flood — so the edge is optional defense-in-depth… orthogonal to the split… not a dependency of it.

tracks.title: What isn't built
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what isn't built. The plane split is real and shipped. Several of the things you'd want around it are still plan… not module. First — ACME is not built. There is no Acme module — the grep returns nothing. Automatic cert issuance and renewal is a planned phase. Today, certificates are installed manually. The SNI machinery is real… what feeds it certs automatically is not. Second — the registry is not durable. The domain table is fresh ETS on every boot. A restart forgets which hosts were attached. The cert files persist on disk… but the rows that map host to app are gone. Third — no attach flow yet. Nothing in the runtime calls attach except tests. The primitives work… the wizard that drives them for you doesn't exist. Fourth — no rate limiting on the content plane yet. The plan names the tools. The checklist item is unchecked. And fifth — one node is one blast radius. The planes share a process and a machine… so a crash is a shared crash. The mitigation is that the modules are kept separable — the content plane could become its own node later with zero redesign. That escape hatch is designed in… not yet exercised. None of this weakens the core claim. An anonymous request can't reach your engine… because the routes aren't there.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can a public visitor reach my agents or secrets? No — and not because a rule says no. The content plane has no route to the Dock, no build route, no agent route, no secret route. Those functions are absent… and non-GET requests have nothing to match at all. Do I need nginx or Caddy in front? Not between the planes — that's the whole point. One node runs both surfaces and serves any number of custom domains itself. An edge CDN in front is optional. What's the x-served-by header I keep seeing? An honesty marker — a standing, externally verifiable claim about what served you. Why does my unknown test domain fail TLS instead of four-oh-four-ing? Because the gate works before HTTP exists. No cert… no handshake… no HTTP layer to return a four-oh-four on. [chuckles] Strangers get no session and no information to probe. And — is the control plane on the public internet? It can be reachable… but locked is not hidden. It's gated by a bearer secret — wrong or absent gets a flat four-oh-one, no dev fallback.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's planes. Two HTTP surfaces on one node. Control — authed, and it does things. Content — anonymous, GET-only, and it serves bytes. The wall between them isn't a proxy you can misconfigure… it's the absence of a road. And the reverse proxy you thought you needed… was one function all along — backed by ETS, and doubling as the bouncer. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under nexus — lesson zero two — where isolation is software, and the security model lives. Planes are simply its inbound face.
